tagline: A winding road through goldfields, then hill crests toward Canada
intro: The Taylor Highway winds through the Fortymile goldfields on a narrow road with steep grades. Alaska DOT includes the Taylor and Top of the World highways in its scenic-byway program, highlighting mountain views, the Fortymile River and old mine workings. Leaving Tetlin Junction, the drive offers views of the Alaska Range and Mentasta Mountains. The Fortymile River system has National Wild and Scenic River status, and the Taylor Highway provides access to it.

Wagon trails supplied Eagle, Chicken and the Fortymile Mining District in the nineteenth century. The Fortymile Road was established in 1951 and later renamed for Ike P. Taylor. The Taylor Highway continues to Eagle; at Jack Wade Junction it also connects with the Top of the World Highway for seasonal road access to Dawson City.

Begin at Tetlin Junction on the Alaska Highway and follow the Taylor toward Chicken. At Jack Wade Junction, turn east onto the Top of the World Highway toward the Canadian border. That road takes its name from its course along hill crests, with views down into the valleys. Old mine workings mark the journey toward Boundary; beyond the border, the highway continues to West Dawson on the Yukon River.

moments.title: Chicken
moments.text: Chicken began as a gold-mining settlement in the late nineteenth century, and mining remains part of its life. Active gold mines and inactive dredges share the area. The Pedro Dredge gives that machinery a particular history: built in California, it was shipped to Pedro Creek north of Fairbanks in 1938. After operating there until 1958, it was dismantled, trucked to Chicken and reassembled the following year. Its last cleanup came in October 1967; in 1998 the 500-ton dredge moved overland to Chicken Gold Camp. The surrounding historic district includes buildings dating from the early 1900s.

moments.title: Jack Wade
moments.text: In 1936 the Yukon Placer Mining Company bought a bucket-line dredge at Franklin, dismantled it and hauled it by horse over the ice to Jack Wade Creek. The creek took its name from Jack Anderson and Wade Nelson, the original claim locators. Its first claims date to 1892. Uncertainty over whether claims lay in Alaska or Canada led many miners to file in both Eagle and Dawson City. Jack Wade had a post office from 1901 until 1948. In 1938, Fred Whitehead held the contract to build the small airstrip at Jack Wade Creek.

moments.title: Poker Creek–Little Gold Creek Border Crossing
moments.text: A painted line inside the joint inspection building marks the United States–Canada border. The two countries built the shared facility in 2001, bringing their inspectors into one building. Earlier travelers faced a different arrangement: American inspections took place in Tok, about 120 miles away, until a log cabin-style station was built at the border in 1971. This is North America’s northernmost international border crossing, on the highway linking Chicken with Dawson. The Top of the World Highway continues east to a ferry terminal in West Dawson, on the Yukon River’s western bank.

practical: Poker Creek–Little Gold Creek Border Crossing: The highways have no winter maintenance, steep narrow grades and long gaps between services. The border crossing operates only in summer. (checked 2026-10-11)
